records.sourceFile: Structural brain differences in professional Australian rules footballers following mild traumatic brain injury - When head size matters.pdf

sourceVerification.doiVerification: DOI printed in the local PDF text.

records.evidenceSummary: Case-control MRI study of 31 male professional Australian rules footballers scanned within 3 months of a suspected concussion (17 scanned within 12 days, 14 later) and 37 healthy male non-athlete controls matched for age. Players had lower proportional hippocampal and amygdala volumes than controls, and the bilateral hippocampal differences stayed significant after Bonferroni correction. Players also had lower right lateral orbitofrontal cortical thickness (an exploratory finding). Results depended on the intracranial volume method: only the right hippocampus differed when volumes were normalized to segmentation-based or supratentorial volume. In 12 players with follow-up scans, no subcortical volume changed significantly after correction.
records.limitations: Controls were non-athletes and players had unknown prior concussion history, so injury and sport exposure cannot be separated. Most ROI results are uncorrected p-values and depend on the choice of intracranial volume estimate, and the longitudinal subset was only 12 players.
records.synthesisCaution: Staff could read the smaller hippocampus as proof that concussion causes lasting brain damage or future neurodegeneration. The design cannot show that the difference came from injury rather than pre-existing or sport-related differences, and the authors show the result changes with the head-size method used.

verification.residualConcerns: Concussion imaging paper; claims checked against Results, Table 3 and Limitations. High priority only because the topic is clinically sensitive.

records.sourceFile: Subtypes of sport-related concussion - A systematic review and meta-cluster analysis.pdf

sourceVerification.doiVerification: DOI printed in the local PDF text.

records.evidenceSummary: A systematic review and meta-cluster analysis of 22 studies (5,592 athletes with sport-related concussion) searched in Medline, Embase, PsycINFO and SPORTDiscus up to December 2018. Multiple correspondence analysis of the reported symptom clusters identified five clusters (migraine, cognitive-emotional, sleep-emotional, neurological and undefined feelings), and 19 studies linked these clusters to clinical outcomes, most often longer recovery.
records.limitations: Most included studies had limitations, and only 13.6% used exploratory data-driven clustering, so analysis bias may have shaped the clusters. The clusters were derived from published reports rather than individual data, the included athletes were mostly adolescents, and the review does not show that subtype-specific treatment improves recovery.
records.synthesisCaution: Staff could treat the five clusters as proven concussion subtypes that should drive treatment choice; no included study tested subtype-targeted management, and the authors note it remains unclear which clusters relate to impairments in particular functional domains.

changes: synthesisCaution: attributed to the authors a statement that subtype-targeted management is untested, which they do not make (they argue the findings 'strongly support a transition' to targeted management) -> states the review did not test it and cites what the authors do say ('it remains unclear if and which specific SRC symptom clusters are associated with impairments in particular functional domains')

paper.practicalImplications: 'in the first week' timing not supported by the findings and the assessment list did not match the authors' recommendation -> removed timing; list now follows 'systematic assessment of at least headache characteristics, neurocognitive functioning, emotional functioning, neurological functioning, and sleep'
paper.limitations: covariate adjustment made specific and added the one-month window ('only five of the included studies adjusted for covariates'; 'within 1 month post-injury')
verification.residualConcerns: Year 2020 taken from the copyright line ('The Author(s) 2020'); no volume, issue or pages are printed. The authors describe the evidence as 'robust' although most included studies had high relative risk of bias.
